source.title: Redundancy and Concept Analysis for Code-trained Language Models
source.authors: Arushi Sharma; Zefu Hu; Christopher J. Quinn; Ali Jannesari

record.file_problem: None; the full paper is present, with some tables flattened in the text extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses LCA and activation visualization to identify code-model neurons associated with code-token classes, and reports specific neurons responding to more than one class. This is a different measurement from the original vision-neuron examples.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports neuron pruning, task accuracy, and layer-similarity results, but these do not measure polysemanticity and are not rows here. The reported neuron examples are selected examples, not an estimate of how prevalent mixed responses are.
record.test_reason: The paper does not test any version. Its 'neurons' are hidden-state dimensions taken from every layer's output via NeuroX (13 layers × 768 = 9984), not MLP neurons. Its polysemantic cases are a few hand-picked, probe-selected units shown as top words or visualizations, with no prevalence estimate, no layer comparison and no baseline. The authors call superposition beyond scope and say confirmation would need further experiments. V2 names a large share of MLP neurons, so these anecdotes measure a related but different thing and go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors trace selected neurons to code properties, identifying 'number', 'string' and higher-level 'text' neurons, and give a few polysemantic or superposition-like examples. They stress that overlapping representations make firm conclusions hard and that superposition is beyond their scope. The paper's main conclusions are about redundancy: over 95% of neurons can be removed without significant accuracy loss.
record.recipe_differences: The study applies LCA, token-class probing, and activation visualization to code-trained models; it does not reproduce the original vision-neuron analysis or the SoLU method.

fits_no_version.finding: Probe-selected hidden-state dimensions in code-trained transformers respond to tokens from more than one syntactic class (CodeBERT L0:47, CodeGPTJava L5:305; possibly CodeBERT L7:717). Others look monosemantic (CodeGPTPy L5:519, numbers). These are selected examples with no count or baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual residual-stream (layer-output) dimensions of code language models, selected by probe weights, can be associated with multiple token classes.

record.peer_reviewed: 2024 39th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering Workshops (ASEW)
record.problems: The concept analysis gives selected examples rather than a prevalence estimate. The authors explicitly note interpretive ambiguity, including that a mixed neuron may reflect superposition, a higher-level concept, or noise. The paper also identifies probing and neuron-ranking limitations and potential confounders.
record.rows_left_out: No additional explicit neuron-to-concept findings were included from Table 6 where the flattened text does not make the associated classes clear. Pruning and CKA results in Tables 4–5 and Figure 3 were omitted because they do not measure polysemanticity.

untested.parts: The share of polysemantic MLP neurons and differences across layers; only selected residual-stream units are shown.
Superposition is defined but not tested; the authors call it beyond scope.
Not tested; model comparisons concern redundancy and accuracy, not the share of polysemantic neurons.
The 'text neuron' reading of L5:305 is raised as a possibility only.

missing.what: Table 6 also lists top-5 words for GraphCodeBERT L5:246 (boolean, CUSTOM, static, "default", "gzip"; mixed type, modifier, string and identifier) and RoBERTa L12:654 (protected, private, 64, 'o', '0'; modifier, number, string), plus UniXCoder L0:625 (END, byte, R, range, U). These are mixed-class examples not recorded as rows.

record.verdict_notes: In this paper, neurons means NeuroX hidden-state activations across all layers (9984 = 13 × 768), not MLP neurons. The polysemanticity examples are illustrative and cherry-picked. The reader's V2 'supports' label is dropped because the study gives no prevalence and does not measure MLP neurons.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not estimate the share of polysemantic neurons, establish that it is large, or compare prevalence across layers. Its concept examples are from code-trained models and token classes, not a broad survey of unrelated language-model contexts.
The paper defines superposition but does not test whether capacity pressure causes the reported mixed activations.
No experiment tests polysemanticity caused by initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.

The paper compares models and tasks for other analyses, but does not measure changes in polysemantic-neuron prevalence due to architecture, activation function, or regularization, nor the performance cost of lowering that prevalence.

The authors suggest that one mixed neuron could be a higher-level text neuron, but do not establish that its activations share a feature the model uses or show that apparently unrelated mixtures are generally coherent.
No comparison varies activation range or explanation-scoring method to test measurement dependence.

rows.subject: CodeBERT
rows.operation_detail: LCA-selected neuron activation visualization for token classes
rows.value: The neuron is reported to activate for IDENTIFIER and NUMBER tokens, with negative activation values for identifiers and positive values for numbers.
rows.note: The authors describe this as a polysemantic example; the figure uses activation visualization.
rows.check: This is a single selected hidden-state dimension, not an MLP neuron, with no baseline. It is negative for identifiers and positive for numbers, so one signed direction separates two classes; that is not clearly unrelated mixed responses. It cannot speak to how common polysemantic neurons are.

rows.subject: CodeBERT
rows.operation_detail: LCA-selected neuron activation visualization for token classes
rows.value: The neuron is described as primarily responsible for STRING tokens, but it also highlights a parenthesis.
rows.note: The authors say the additional activation could indicate polysemanticity or noise.
rows.check: This is a selected hidden-state dimension. The extra activation is one parenthesis, which the authors say may be noise. The figure alone cannot show polysemanticity.

rows.subject: CodeGPTJava
rows.operation_detail: LCA-based tracing of an important neuron to token classes
rows.measure: Top words and associated token classes
rows.value: The neuron is reported as responsible for both KEYWORD and IDENTIFIER tokens.
rows.note: The authors say this may indicate superposition or may be interpreted as a higher-level monosemantic “text neuron.”
rows.check: This is a selected residual-stream dimension. Its top words mix keywords and identifiers, and the authors offer a monosemantic 'text neuron' reading as an alternative. It is anecdotal, with no prevalence estimate.

rows.subject: CodeGPTPy
rows.operation_detail: LCA-based tracing of an important neuron to token classes
rows.measure: Top words and associated token class
rows.value: The neuron is described as the cleanest example of a monosemantic number neuron; its listed top words are 79, 104, 78, 118, and 99.
rows.note: This is a contrasting example, not evidence about the prevalence of mixed neurons.
rows.check: This is a contrast example of a monosemantic 'number' dimension. 'Absent' wrongly implies a test of V2. A single selected monosemantic unit says nothing about how many neurons are polysemantic.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
